ACCEPTThe new note is valid as stated for  $r\ge2$  and  $t\ge1$ . The exact dissociation formula, preservation of literal inclusion-minimality, degree and connectivity values, fixed-connectivity asymptotic sharpness, and the  $\beta_2=n/2$  counterexamples all follow.The two boundaries identified in the note are real: isolated old vertices can invalidate the padding formula at  $t=1$ , and the balanced base graph at  $r=1$  has dissociation number  $8$ , not  $7$ . Neither causes a defect under the stated hypotheses.This is a paper review of the supplied text. I use the general selected-set  $n/12$  bound as stipulated and rederive the prior family’s exact dissociation formula below.1. The padding formula exhausts all dissociation setsLet  $H$  have fixed nonempty bipartition classes  $A,B$ , and let  $J=J_t(H)$ . Write
$$a_0=|A|,\qquad b_0=|B|.$$
The new classes are  $X$  on the  $A$ -side and  $Y$  on the  $B$ -side, each of size  $t$ .The three claimed lower bounds are valid:An old maximum dissociation set remains dissociation because the graph induced on the old vertices is unchanged. $A\cup X$  is independent and has size  $a_0+t$ . $B\cup Y$  is independent and has size  $b_0+t$ .For the upper bound, take an arbitrary dissociation set  $D$ . There is no restriction on which old vertices it retains.Case 1:  $D\cap(X\cup Y)=\varnothing$ . Then  $D$  is a dissociation set in  $H$ , so
$$|D|\le\beta_2(H).$$
Now suppose  $D\cap X\ne\varnothing$ . Any chosen  $x\in X$  is adjacent to every vertex in  $B\cup Y$ . Consequently,
$$|D\cap(B\cup Y)|\le1.$$
Case 2:  $D\cap(B\cup Y)=\varnothing$ . Then
$$D\subseteq A\cup X,\qquad |D|\le a_0+t.$$
Case 3: the unique opposite-side vertex belongs to  $Y$ . That vertex is adjacent to every vertex of  $A\cup X$ , so at most one vertex of  $A\cup X$  can belong to  $D$ . Thus
$$|D|\le2\le a_0+t.$$
The last inequality holds even at the smallest permitted values  $a_0=t=1$ .Case 4: the unique opposite-side vertex is an old  $b\in B$ . Since  $b$  is adjacent to all of  $X$ , exactly one vertex of  $X$  belongs to  $D$ . Its edge to  $b$  uses the degree-one allowance of  $b$ , so every chosen old  $A$ -vertex must avoid  $N_H(b)$ . Hence
$$|D|\le a_0-\deg_H(b)+2.$$
Under the no-isolate hypothesis,
$$|D|\le a_0+1\le a_0+t.$$
Case 5:  $D\cap X=\varnothing$  and  $D\cap Y\ne\varnothing$ . The symmetric argument gives
$$|D|\le b_0+t.$$
These cases are exhaustive. Therefore
$$\boxed{\beta_2(J_t(H))
=\max\bigl(\beta_2(H),\,|A|+t,\,|B|+t\bigr).}$$
In particular, the proof works at  $t=1$ . The inequality that needs attention there is exactly the use of  $\deg_H(b)\ge1$ , and it is available under the lemma’s stated hypothesis.2. Isolated old vertices: the stated counterexample is correctIf  $A=\{a\}$ ,  $B=\{b\}$ , and  $H$  has no edges, then  $J_1(H)$  has exactly the edges
$$ay,\quad yx,\quad xb.$$
It is the four-vertex path  $a-y-x-b$ .The set  $\{a,b,x\}$  induces just the edge  $bx$ , so it is a dissociation set of size  $3$ . All four vertices are not dissociation because the two internal vertices of the path have degree two. Thus
$$\beta_2(J_1(H))=3,$$
whereas
$$\beta_2(H)=|A|+1=|B|+1=2.$$
So the warning in the note is exact: the no-isolate hypothesis cannot simply be removed from a statement covering  $t=1$ .The same case split locates the boundary completely. For arbitrary  $H$  with nonempty parts, define
$$d_A=\min_{a\in A}\deg_H(a),\qquad
d_B=\min_{b\in B}\deg_H(b).$$
Then, without a no-isolate assumption,
$$\boxed{
\beta_2(J_t(H))
=
\max\left\{
\beta_2(H),\
|A|+t,\
|B|+t,\
|A|+2-d_B,\
|B|+2-d_A
\right\}.
}
\tag{*}$$
The two additional bounds are attained. For example, choose  $b\in B$  of minimum degree and one  $x\in X$ ; then
$$\{x,b\}\cup\bigl(A\setminus N_H(b)\bigr)$$
induces exactly the edge  $xb$  and has size  $|A|+2-d_B$ . The other side is symmetric.This also shows:For  $t\ge2$ , the two additional terms in  $(*)$  are absorbed by  $|A|+t$  and  $|B|+t$ , even if old isolates exist.For  $t=1$ , old isolates can produce the extra terms  $|A|+2$  or  $|B|+2$ .This is a clarification of the hypothesis’s role, not a required correction.There is also an important distinction in the application: the  $2r$  selected isolates in  $G_{r,r}[S]$  are not isolated vertices of  $G_{r,r}$ . Each is a pendant vertex in the full old graph. Thus the base graph satisfies the padding lemma’s no-isolate hypothesis.3. Literal minimality survives, including the newly omitted vertexFor a selected set  $Q$ , an outside vertex  $v$  is formed precisely when either: $v$  has two distinct neighbours in  $Q$ ; or $v$  has a neighbour  $q\in Q$  that has another neighbour in  $Q$ .These are the two possible positions of  $v$  in the required  $K_{1,2}$ .For every  $Q\subseteq S$  and every old vertex  $v\notin Q$ ,
$$v\text{ is formed by }Q\text{ in }H
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v\text{ is formed by }Q\text{ in }J_t(H).
\tag{1}$$
Indeed, a formation triple for this target consists of the old vertex  $v$  and two vertices of  $Q$ , which are also old. All edges among those three vertices are unchanged.This observation handles literal minimality directly.First,  $S$  forms the extension:Every old outside vertex retains its old formation triple.Every  $x\in X$  has at least two selected neighbours in  $B$ .Every  $y\in Y$  has at least two selected neighbours in  $A$ .Second, for every  $s\in S$ , old minimality supplies an old vertex
$$v_s\in V(H)\setminus(S\setminus\{s\})$$
that is unformed by  $S\setminus\{s\}$ . By (1), that vertex remains unformed in the extension.Crucially,  $v_s$  may equal  $s$ . The proof does not restrict the witness to vertices originally outside  $S$ . Thus it includes exactly the newly omitted selected vertices required by literal minimality.Formation is upward closed: if a set forms, every larger selected set forms. Therefore failure of every single deletion proves inclusion-minimality.For the supplied base family, the deletion table remains valid verbatim, using the prior proof’s names:Deleted vertexUnformed old vertexPersistent reason $x_i$  $u_i$ Its only selected neighbour  $l_i$  becomes isolated in the selected graph. $l_i$  $u_i$ It has no selected neighbour. $h_i$  $v_i$ Its only selected neighbour is the selected isolate  $p_i$ . $p_i$  $p_i$ The newly omitted vertex has no selected neighbour.All added vertices remain outside the selection. Consequently, their new edges cannot supply either of the two selected vertices needed to repair these failures.The selected induced graph is unchanged, so the counts of selected stars, edges and isolates are preserved exactly.4. The prior family’s unrestricted formula is correctThe new note’s six-vertex blocks are the prior family’s blocks after the relabelling
$$(x,l,h,p,u,v)\longleftrightarrow(c,l,m,i,p,h).$$
The cross edges are also the same complete bipartite coupling between the two witness groups.Here is the unrestricted dissociation calculation for  $G_{a,b}$ , with  $c=a+b$ .Let
$$W_A=\{u_i,v_i:i\le a\},\qquad
W_B=\{u_i,v_i:i>a\}.$$
These witness classes induce  $K_{2a,2b}$ . For any dissociation set  $D$ , the four possibilities give:Witness classes met by  $D$ Upper boundNeither $3c$  $W_A$  only $4a+3b$  $W_B$  only $3a+4b$ Both $3c+2$ Each bound has the stated justification.No witnessesEach block contributes at most two vertices from its selected  $P_3$ , together with at most the selected isolate  $p_i$ . Thus it contributes at most three.Witnesses on only one sideFor a first-group block, the two disjoint triples
$$\{x_i,l_i,u_i\},\qquad \{p_i,v_i,h_i\}$$
each induce a  $P_3$ . A dissociation set contains at most two vertices from each triple, hence at most four vertices from the block.There is an additional edge between the triples, but this cannot invalidate an upper bound obtained from their separate restrictions.A second-group block contains no selected witness in this case, so contributes at most three. This gives  $4a+3b$ , and the reverse case is symmetric.Witnesses on both sidesBecause all cross edges are present, meeting both witness classes forces
$$|D\cap W_A|=|D\cap W_B|=1.$$
Otherwise a chosen witness would have at least two chosen neighbours across the complete bipartite graph.The two chosen witnesses are in different blocks and are adjacent to each other. Each therefore has no remaining degree allowance for an old neighbour.If the chosen witness in a block is  $u_i$ , then  $l_i$  is absent. At most  $x_i,h_i,p_i,u_i$  remain: four vertices.If it is  $v_i$ , then  $h_i,p_i$  are absent. At most  $x_i,l_i,v_i$  remain: three vertices.All other blocks have no witnesses and contribute at most three. Hence the total is at most  $3c+2$ .AttainmentThe supplied attaining sets have no overlooked edges.For  $4a+3b$ , choose
$$\{x_i,p_i,u_i,v_i\}$$
in first-group blocks and
$$\{l_i,h_i,p_i\}$$
in second-group blocks. The only induced edges are the first-group edges  $p_iv_i$ . This attains  $4a+3b$ ; reversing the groups attains  $3a+4b$ .For  $3c+2$ , choose one block from each group. In those two blocks select
$$\{x_i,h_i,p_i,u_i\},$$
and in every other block select  $\{l_i,h_i,p_i\}$ . The induced edges are the two edges  $x_ih_i$  and the single cross edge between the two chosen  $u_i$ ’s. They are disjoint.Therefore
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G_{a,b})=3(a+b)+\max(a,b,2).}$$
This calculation applies to every dissociation set; it does not impose a leaf-retention constraint.The  $r\ge2$  boundaryPutting  $a=b=r$  gives
$$\beta_2(G_{r,r})=6r+\max(r,2).$$
Consequently,
$$\beta_2(G_{r,r})=
\begin{cases}
8,&r=1,\\
7r,&r\ge2.
\end{cases}$$
Thus the new note correctly excludes  $r=1$ . More explicitly, padding the exceptional graph gives
$$\beta_2(J_t(G_{1,1}))=\max(8,6+t).$$
At  $t=1$ , this is  $8$ , whereas extending the displayed main formula to  $r=1$  would incorrectly give  $7$ .For  $r\ge2$ , the base graph has:
$$|V|=12r,\qquad |S|=8r,\qquad |A|=|B|=6r,
\qquad |S\cap A|=|S\cap B|=4r.$$
It is connected through the complete bipartite witness graph, has no isolated vertices, and has the selected  $p_i$ ’s as pendant vertices. All hypotheses used in the new note are therefore satisfied.5. The minimum degree and vertex connectivity are exactly  $t+1$ Consider the stated general connectivity lemma:  $H$  is connected, bipartite, and has a pendant vertex.Every old degree increases by exactly  $t$ . Since  $\delta(H)=1$ , all old vertices have degree at least  $t+1$ , with equality at an old pendant vertex. The new degrees are
$$|B|+t,\qquad |A|+t,$$
both at least  $t+1$ . Hence
$$\boxed{\delta(J_t(H))=t+1.}$$
For connectivity, both directions are valid.Lower boundLet  $C$  be a set of at most  $t$  deleted vertices.If both  $X\setminus C$  and  $Y\setminus C$  are nonempty, their surviving complete bipartite graph is connected. Every surviving old  $A$ -vertex attaches to a surviving vertex of  $Y$ , and every surviving old  $B$ -vertex attaches to a surviving vertex of  $X$ . Thus the entire remaining graph is connected.If  $X\subseteq C$ , then  $|X|=t$  and  $|C|\le t$  force
$$C=X.$$
In particular, no old vertex and no  $Y$ -vertex has been deleted. The whole connected graph  $H$  survives, and each vertex of  $Y$  attaches to the nonempty class  $A$ . The remainder is connected.The case  $Y\subseteq C$  is symmetric. Therefore
$$\kappa(J_t(H))\ge t+1.$$
This includes  $t=1$ : deleting the sole vertex of  $X$  or the sole vertex of  $Y$  leaves the whole connected old graph available.Upper bound and the surviving-vertex issueLet  $p\in A$  be an old pendant vertex with unique old neighbour  $q\in B$ . Its neighbourhood in the extension is
$$N_J(p)=\{q\}\cup Y,$$
of size  $t+1$ .Delete this neighbourhood. Then  $p$  is isolated. Moreover, every vertex of  $X$  survives, and  $X\ne\varnothing$ . Thus at least one other vertex survives alongside  $p$ : this is a genuine disconnecting cut, not a deletion leaving a single vertex.Hence
$$\kappa(J_t(H))\le t+1.$$
Combining the two directions,
$$\boxed{\kappa(J_t(H))=\delta(J_t(H))=t+1.}$$
Maximum degree in  $P_{r,t}$ For  $H=G_{r,r}$ , both old parts have size  $6r$ , so every old degree is at most  $6r$ . After padding, every old degree is at most  $6r+t$ , while every new vertex has degree exactly  $6r+t$ . Therefore
$$\boxed{\Delta(P_{r,t})=6r+t.}$$
There is no exceptional case at  $t=1$ .6. The exact formulas and all gap regimes agreeCombining the base calculation, padding lemma and minimality preservation gives
$$\begin{aligned}
n&=12r+2t,\\
|S|&=8r,\\
\beta_2(P_{r,t})&=\max(7r,6r+t),\\
\delta(P_{r,t})&=\kappa(P_{r,t})=t+1,\\
\Delta(P_{r,t})&=6r+t.
\end{aligned}$$
The selected graph consists of exactly  $2r$  copies of  $P_3$  and  $2r$  isolates, with no selected edge component.The gap calculation is exact:
$$8r-\max(7r,6r+t)=\min(r,2r-t).$$
Its parameter regimes are:Range $\beta_2(P_{r,t})$ Selected gap $1\le t\le r$  $7r$  $r$  $r<t<2r$  $6r+t$  $2r-t>0$  $t=2r$  $8r$  $0$  $t>2r$  $6r+t$  $2r-t<0$ Thus the theorem correctly gives an exact gap for every  $t\ge1$ ; positivity holds precisely when  $t<2r$ .In particular,  $t=1$  gives gap  $r$  and
$$\delta=\kappa=2$$
for every  $r\ge2$ .7. Fixed-connectivity asymptotic sharpness followsFix an integer  $h\ge2$  and put  $t=h-1$ . For
$$r\ge\max(2,t),$$
we have  $t\le r$ , so
$$|S|-\beta_2=r,\qquad
n=12r+2(h-1),\qquad
\delta=\kappa=h.$$
Therefore
$$\frac{|S|-\beta_2}{n}
=
\frac{r}{12r+2(h-1)}
\longrightarrow\frac1{12}.$$
Together with the stipulated upper bound for the specified minimal selected-star/edge/isolate selections,
$$|S|-\beta_2\le\left\lfloor\frac n{12}\right\rfloor,$$
this proves the claimed asymptotic sharpness under any fixed lower bound on both minimum degree and vertex connectivity.The maximum degree is
$$6r+h-1,$$
so the construction has precisely the limitation stated in the note concerning maximum degree.The assertion about unrounded equality is also correct. For every  $t\ge1$ ,
$$|S|-\beta_2\le r
<
r+\frac t6
=
\frac n{12}.$$
Thus no padded graph attains unrounded equality.It can nevertheless attain the rounded bound. For example, when  $1\le t\le5$  and  $r\ge\max(2,t)$ ,
$$\left\lfloor\frac n{12}\right\rfloor
=r
=|S|-\beta_2.$$
This is compatible with an obstruction specifically to equality with  $n/12$ .8. The  $\beta_2=n/2$  counterexamples are validBecause
$$\frac n2=6r+t,$$
the exact formula yields
$$\beta_2-\frac n2=\max(r-t,0).$$
Thus, throughout this family,
$$\boxed{\beta_2=n/2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t\ge r.}$$
Combining this with the gap calculation shows that  $\beta_2=n/2$  and a positive selected gap coexist exactly in the range
$$r\le t<2r.$$
At the chosen value  $t=r$ ,
$$n=14r,\qquad
\beta_2=7r=\frac n2,\qquad
|S|=8r,$$
and
$$\delta=\kappa=r+1,\qquad \Delta=7r.$$
These give arbitrarily high minimum degree and vertex connectivity as  $r\to\infty$ .The proposed strengthening fails by the stated amount:
$$4\beta_2=28r
\quad<\quad
2|S|+n=16r+14r=30r.$$
Equivalently, when  $\beta_2=n/2$ , that strengthening would require
$$|S|\le n/2,$$
whereas this selection has size  $8r>7r$ .For completeness, the exact difference for the whole padded family is
$$4\beta_2-(2|S|+n)
=
\begin{cases}
-2t,&1\le t\le r,\\[2mm]
2(t-2r),&t\ge r.
\end{cases}$$
So the strengthening fails throughout  $1\le t<2r$ , is an equality at  $t=2r$ , and holds for this family when  $t>2r$ .The two parameter choices have distinct consequences: fixed  $t$  establishes the  $1/12$  asymptotic coefficient, while  $t=r$  establishes the growing-connectivity  $\beta_2=n/2$  counterexamples, whose selected gap ratio is  $1/14$ . The note keeps those consequences separate correctly.All accepted conclusions concern the specified minimal selection  $S$ .
